content:
That the Property should be
added to the Council’s list of Assets of Community
Value.
 
Reasons for recommendations

1.     
Local authorities are required to maintain a list of
Assets of Community Value pursuant to Part 5 of the Localism Act
2011 (“the Act”).

2.     
Under section 88 of the Act, an asset of community
value means buildings or land where, in the opinion of the
authority, the current use or use in recent past furthers the
social wellbeing or social interests of the local community and it
is realistic to think that there can continue to be use of the
buildings or land which will further the social wellbeing or social
interests of the local community within the next five years.The
Property is located within the Council’s boundary.

3.     
The nominating body is a charity, being a community
interest group with a local connection and therefore is a
qualifying body within regulation 5(1) of the Assets of Community
Value (England) Regulations 2012 (“the
Regulations”).

4.     
The Property is not within the categories excluded
from listing within the Regulations and a place of worship can
qualify as an asset of community value.

5.     
It is reasonable to conclude that the evidence
submitted sufficiently demonstrates that the Property is used or
has recently been used in a manner which furthers social wellbeing
or social interests of the local community and it is realistic to
think it could continue to do so within the next five
years.
 
Other
options considered and rejected
Not to add the Property to the
Council’s list of Assets of Community Value.

content:
The Director of Property and
Planning, Gayle Wootton, presented a report detailing proposed
changes to the Council’s Constitution, some which required
consideration by the Audit and Governance Committee and approval by
Council (outlined at Appendix 1), and some proposed changes which
fell within the delegation to the Monitoring Officer (outlined at
Appendix 2).
 
The Committee were asked to
provide comments and feedback on the proposed changes in Appendix
1, as follows:
 

·        
Corporate Parenting – removing the reference in the current Constitution to
the council as a corporate parent, as the district council
functions do not include a responsibility as a corporate parent and
this reference was not included in the Constitution prior to May
2025.
 
It
was acknowledged that Chorley Council provides many services which
benefit children in care and care leavers, however in terms of
governance the council does not legally hold that
responsibility.
 

·        
Proposed Change to regarding the Procedure before
Planning Committee - The current
constitution says that ‘about one week before the Planning
Committee is to meet, all those with the right to make a request to
speak will be informed of their opportunity to do so by the
Council’.
 
In
practice, ‘all those with the right to make a request to
speak’ means every member of the public, and not just those
who live near to an application or who may be affected by it. It is
therefore impractical to notify everyone and therefore the proposal
is to change the Constitution to notify only those who have made a
representation on the application, which is current
practice.
 

·        
Proposed Changes to the Waiver Process
- The proposal is to amend the contract
procedure rules in respect of the requirement to obtain approval
for waivers of the rules. This means approval would not be required
from a Cabinet Member for intermediate value contracts
(£30,000-£180,000) (Paragraph 39.3) and high value
contracts (above £180,001) would no longer require Cabinet
approval (Paragraph 39.4).

 
Gayle Wootton
stressed that waiver process was an operational matter and that the
Cabinet Member would still be involved in the decision-making
process for project budget approval and award of
contract.  The proposals aimed to
remove duplication and streamline the process.
 
The Committee
indicated that it was important that members still have oversight
of the waiver process to identify any issues relating to
contracts. Gayle Wootton highlighted that waivers of
contract procedure rules will
continue to be reported to the
Audit and Governance Committee to monitor any trends and identify
any concerns.

 

 
The report also informed
members of future changes to the Constitution which will be brought
to a future meeting. These were:
 

·        
Changes to decision making in the Leisure Company,
following a recent audit

·        
Government proposals to change the types of planning
applications that can be dealt with at Planning
Committee
 
 
Resolved –
 
i)                   
It was noted that, following consideration by
this Committee, the proposed changes to the Constitution set out at
Appendix 1 would be submitted to Council for approval in
September.
ii)                 
That the changes at Appendix 2 that fall within
the delegation to the Monitoring Officer be noted.

Recommendations
approved.
 
Reasons for recommendations:

The grant funding
will enable the business to further develop and support their
sustainable practices and carbon reduction through the production
of cleaner cheaper energy and use of more energy efficient
machinery. It will assist with the delivery of the following
outcomes:

·        
Reduction in fossil fuel use
·        
Reduction in greenhouse gas emissions
·        
Production of cheaper, green energy
 

The proposals support
the Council’s Net Zero Policy.

 
Other
options considered and rejected:

Other options considered
include:

a)     
Not awarding the funding. The option of not granting
this application will have long-term impacts. Without the grant
funding, the business would be unable to afford the purchase and
installation of the solar panel system upgrades, invertors and
storage batteries. This would mean continued inefficiencies, higher
energy costs, and further reduce the effectiveness of their current
solar panels, limiting the environmental and financial benefits
they can provide.
b)    
Awarding a lesser amount of funding. Similar to
above, only awarding part of the funding would mean the business
couldn’t fully implement the project and would not receive
all of the benefits that the full project would bring.

content:
Planning permission refused for
the following reason:
 
‘The proposal offers
limited off-street car parking provision
and given the lack of on-street parking in the immediate area the
proposal results in an intensification of the use of the site that
will lead to an increase in demand for on-street parking in the
area to the detriment of highway safety in the local area. The
intensification of the use and the requirement to accommodate
refuse and cycle storage results in the provision of limited
amenity space for future residents which will be detrimental to
their amenity.  The increased intensity
of the proposed use will also lead an increase of activity beyond
that of a family home and as a result this will have an
unacceptable impact on the amenity of the neighbouring residential
property. As a result, the proposals are contrary to Policies BNE1
and ST4 of the Chorley Local Plan, and Policies HS10 and EN4 of the
emerging Central Lancashire Local Plan.’

decisions.

content:
Recommendations
approved.
 
Reasons for recommendations

1.     
It is necessary to confirm the immediate Article 4
direction before the 23 March 2026, otherwise the direction will
expire and the permitted development right to materially convert a
dwellinghouse into a small HMO will be restored.

2.     
The confirmation of the immediate Article 4
direction will allow for the continued regulation and monitoring of
HMOs, and for conditions to be attached to planning permissions. It
will continue to improve the Council’s ability to ensure the
management standards of HMOs are maintained.

3.     
Allowing the immediate Article 4 direction to expire
will mean that any future policy in the Central Lancashire Local
Plan or a future Supplementary Planning Document or equivalent,
which has a policy on conversion of dwelling houses to HMOs, would
not apply to conversions for six or fewer residents as these would
have permitted development rights.
 
Other
options considered and rejected
To not confirm the immediate
Article 4 direction and allow the direction to expire on 23 March
2026. This would result in the immediate Article 4 direction no
longer applying and the permitted development right to materially
convert a dwellinghouse into a small HMO to be utilised again. The
Council would not have control of conversions to small HMOs (i.e.
for occupation by between 3 and 6 unrelated people) in the borough.
There is a risk of clusters of HMOs occurring which might impact on
residential amenity and increasing risk of displacement of smaller
HMOs where neighbouring Councils have introduced the
measure.
topline: The Executive Member (Planning and Development) has decided to confirm the immediate Article 4 direction to regulate the conversion of dwelling houses into small HMOs.

Decision
The Executive Member is

£15,000 to UK ICS.
 
Reasons for recommendations
The grant funding will enable
the business to further develop and support their sustainable
practices and carbon reduction through the purchase and
installation of a full heating and air conditioning system for both
floors at their location. This will assist with the delivery of the
following outcomes:
·        
Reduction in fossil fuel use
·        
Reduction in greenhouse gas emissions
·        
Production of cheaper, green energy
 
The proposals support the
Council’s Net Zero Policy
 
Other
options considered and rejected
The option of not granting this
application will have long-term impacts. 
Without the grant funding, they
would be unable to afford both the installation of the heating and
air-conditioning system and the cleaning of the solar panels. This
would mean delaying one or both elements of the project, resulting
in continued inefficiencies, higher energy costs, and an
uncomfortable working environment during extreme weather
conditions. It would also reduce the effectiveness of their solar
panels, limiting the environmental and financial benefits they can
provide.

Depot site can be released without any delays to bring forward the
new residential scheme which is part of the wider Town Centre
Improvement works.

3.     
To mitigate the risk to funding on the Bengal St
Depot project secured through the governments previously titled
Levelling Up Fund.

4.     
Letter of Intent (LOI’s) are widely used in
the construction industry and particularly beneficial for time
sensitive projects which applies to this programme.
 
Other
options considered and rejected
To not undertake the
‘enabling works package’ – This has been rejected
as this would not contribute towards achieving an earlier
completion programme which would impact on delays to the relocation
of the depot services and land release of the Bengal St Depot site
for the new residential scheme.
topline: The Executive Member (Economic Development and Public Service Reform) has decided to approve recommendations for an enabling package of works to manage programme risk and facilitate the release of the Bengal St Depot site for a new residential scheme.

content:
Planning permission refused due
to the following reason:
 
The
proposal fails to provide the necessary level of off-street car parking further exacerbating existing
parking issues in the immediate area. The overly intensive use of
the building because of the number of perspective residents mean
that an inadequate amount of amenity space can be provided to
support the proposed use of the building. Additionally, the
intensive use of the building will have a detrimental impact on the
impact of the first-floor occupant of the building because of noise
and disturbance caused by the proposed use. The proposal is
therefore contrary to Policies BNE1 and ST4 of the Chorley Local
Plan (2015), and Paragraph 135(f) of the National Planning Policy
Framework.
topline: The Planning Committee has decided to refuse planning permission for a building due to concerns over parking, amenity space, and potential noise disturbance.

content:
Planning permission refused due
to the following reason:
 
The
proposed development would be located within the Green Belt as
defined by the Chorley Local Plan 2012 - 2026. The proposed
development is not considered to meet with any of the exceptions to
inappropriate development set out at paragraph 154 and would not
meet with the terms of paragraph 155 of the National Planning
Policy Framework as it would lead to unrestricted sprawl, would
harm the setting of a historic settlement and would not be in a
sustainable location. The proposed development would be
inappropriate development in the Green Belt and therefore
harmful by definition. It is not
considered that there are very special circumstances to overcome
the definitional harm to the Green Belt. The proposal is therefore
contrary to the National Planning Policy Framework.
topline: The Planning Committee has decided to refuse planning permission for a proposed development in the Green Belt area.
